BLUEY: Oh, I'm a big champion of the Article One authority of Congress. So, don't -- we can go down that path. I think Congress should exert more authority when it comes to oversight, whether it's a Republican or a Democrat.

But I think what is important today, and the reason that it's relevant, is, this might not be the last time that the United States finds itself in a situation where we have a global pandemic. And holding that person accountable, getting answers, holding the CCP, the Chinese Communist Party, accountable for what its role was. And then think about all of the losses that our country experienced, not only in terms of jobs, but the schooling. I mean, I have kids. It affected my family's life profoundly.

SEAWRIGHT: Can someone remind me who was in charge when we were going through the Covid-19 pandemic? Because I think sometimes that gets lost in the conversation. Who was the president?

BLUEY: Apparently, Anthony Fauci thought he was.

SEAWRIGHT: Well, who was in charge and who was the president?

HILL: I want to bring -- so I want to -- because I know you two could go on all day, and I do enjoy it. Don't get me wrong.

But, Eleanor, when we look at this, right, people, to Rob's point, people do have questions, right? To Antjuan's point, people are also questioning certain things that are happening right now.

When we look at what has come out in advance, there is no love lost between Rand Paul and Anthony Fauci, as we know.

ELEANOR MUELLER, WHITE HOUSE ECONOMY POLICY REPORTER, "SEMAFOR": Yes.

HILL: What does this -- what does this actually achieve, right, to put all this out ahead of time? And it is really, you can pick and choose who you want. It's certainly not all flattering to Dr. Fauci --

HILL: But it doesn't all either prove what Rand Paul, I think, is hoping to prove.

So, what do we, as the American people, get from this moment? MUELLER: So, for Americans, particularly on the right, who were

frustrated with lockdowns, who thought that guidance on vaccines was misplaced, Anthony Fauci was the place that they directed all of those frustrations into. And so, while there is nothing, to your point, in these 1,100 pages that RFK found on government servers and gave to Rand Paul that would incriminate Fauci, it does stoke those political tensions right as this fifth hearing that Rand Paul has called where he can interrogate Fauci is going to happen.

And so whether or not Fauci does do what Paul wants and says something today that does incriminate himself remains to be seen. I don't know that there's proof in these diaries that he does think that it came from a lab.

MUELLER: He made one comment that maybe alluded to the possibility of the lab being somehow related, but didn't explicitly say something that contradicted himself in the past. And so, it's really more of a bad look, I think, to have him leaning into all of this fame.

SEAWRIGHT: And remember --

HILL: Here's -- I'm going to leave it there because we have more to get to.

SEAWRIGHT: Trump was in charge of Covid.

HILL: But we have more to get to. But it will certainly -- I mean there will be, I think we can all guarantee, no shortage of fireworks this morning or moments that people would like to have go viral. So, we'll be watching all of it for you.

Still ahead here on CNN THIS MORNING, Gavin Newsom's affair with a then staffer reemerging two decades later. How the scandal could impact a potential presidential run.

SEN. RICHARD BLUMENTHAL (D-CT): America stands with Ukraine.

HILL: A win for Ukraine. The U.S. Senate passing a Russian sanctions bill. Can Ukraine's leader now turn this momentum into Patriot missiles?

And the lifeguard who dove into a pounding surf to rescue a boy set to receive a high civilian honor as President Trump offers an invite to the White House.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK) [06:50:41]

HILL: Breaking news overnight, an escalation in the war with Iran. The U.S. and Saudi Arabia joining forces to target Iranian backed militias in Iraq after Iran attempted to launch a surprise missile attack on U.S. bases in the region. Those missiles were intercepted. Iran making its move, of course, while Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, was in Washington, as well as Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, both visiting Trump at the White House on Tuesday.

Zelenskyy also in Washington making his way later in the day to The Hill to watch the U.S. advance -- the Senate advance a sanctions bill for Russia and Iran.

PRESIDENT VOLODYMYR ZELENSKYY, UKRAINE: It's not only about money, how Russia -- how to stop to finance this war, but it's also a big signal to Europe, a big signal to Ukraine, big support of our people.

HILL: Joining me now, David Sanger, White House and national security correspondent for "The New York Times."

DAVID SANGER, CNN POLITICAL AND NATIONAL SECURITY ANALYST: Good morning, Erica.

HILL: I mean, a lot happening in the last -- in the last 24 hours I think is putting it mildly when we look at what is happening on both fronts with Iran and Ukraine.

Let's start, though, if we could, with these attacks overnight and what we saw. The timing cannot be ignored, obviously, but also what has come out of that. The U.S. and Saudi Arabia joining forces now. Can you put this in perspective for us?

SANGER: Sure. So, you know, last time that we discussed this, Erica, we talked about how the president was increasingly trapped by his inability to get out of this war. And I think in the past 24 hours, we've seen why. He stood down over the weekend from what he had threatened would be a massive attack. It looked like we had some peace in the region for a bit. And then, four days into this, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which we believe is really running Iran these days, or is the most influential force there, launches this not very large attack, it was four or fewer missiles, that were at Jordan.

Meanwhile, the Saudis, tired of being attacked by the Houthis and some Iran-backed militias, did some airstrikes in Iraq. And so, you see that this is beginning to spread, or is continuing to spread throughout the region. And the more countries that get involved, the more difficult it gets to unwind this whole thing. So, the whole question right now for the president is, could he even

get the Iranians back to the position they were in a little more than a month ago when he signed that 14-point vaguely written plan that was supposed to launch a bigger negotiation.

HILL: All of this happening, of course, when Benjamin Netanyahu was visiting Washington. There is clearly a disconnect between the president and the prime minister when it comes to where this war goes, right, and what they each would like to see.

What is your takeaway from that meeting, what it says about this relationship right now, as the two are still involved in this war together?

SANGER: We don't know very much about what happened in the meeting yet. I'm sure more of that will begin to seep out. But we do know this. This was the first time the two of them had met since Prime Minister Netanyahu was in Washington prior to the war. And that was the time when he basically convinced President Trump that if they joined together in an attack on Iran, it would be swift, it would overthrow the government, that Iran was so weak that it would crack, and this would be a couple of weeks' operation.

Well, clearly, that turned out to be wrong. And I think the president is now rightly suspicious a bit of Prime Minister Netanyahu's predictions.

HILL: I also want to ask you about President Zelenskyy. So, of course, I noted he was there for, you know, in the Senate yesterday, but also meeting with the president, bringing some wins with him in this moment. You noted, he may actually have those cards now that the president gave him such a hard time about in that infamous Oval Office meeting. Does he have a lot more leverage in this moment?

SANGER: He sure does. And, you know, it really shows you what, you know, a year and a half of change, technological development and just grit will do here.

When he came in February of last year, he didn't have that many cards to play. He was, you know, at best static and maybe losing on the battlefield. They've now developed drones that obviously reach well into Russia, have done significant damage to the Russian oil and gas industry, hit a lot of their refineries, can reach Moscow. And suddenly it was President Zelenskyy who was getting a bit of a warmer reception than Prime Minister Netanyahu. How's that for a reversal of fortunes here?

Now, the president can be a little bit fickle on these things. And, of course, he likes sticking with winners. But it does raise the question of whether the U.S. and the Congress will end up doing more to back the Ukrainians as Lindsey Graham was advocating until his death.

HILL: Yes. It will certainly interesting to watch, as always.

David, always good to talk to you. Thank you.

SANGER: Great to be with you, Erica.

HILL: A former staffer to Gavin Newsom is offering new details of their affair from 20 years ago. Newsom, who at the time was the mayor of San Francisco, admitted to that affair in 2007. An affair with Ruby Rippey. But his rise as a potential 2028 presidential contender is putting this chapter in his life back in the spotlight. He also wrote about it in his book recently. And then in an essay published in "Vanity Fair" yesterday, Rippey says, "for my former boss, it is a footnote in a larger arc of ascent. For me, it is the fracture that split my life into before and after."

The group chat is back.

I will say, she writes in this this "Vanity Fair" piece, it's not written from a victim perspective, right, it's more of a, hey, I'm just letting you all know what happened in this moment. A spokesperson for Newsom put this message out in response, saying the governor had apologized for what had happened and noted that he was, you know, sort of done talking about it. He apologized for it. He's going to move on. He calls it in his memoir, "the briefest of affairs," and recounted how he claimed -- came clean to Rippey's husband, who also worked for Newsom at the time, and was a friend of the mayors. She points out, that's not actually what happened.

How much could this impact Newsom moving forward?

MUELLER: That's the question, right? I mean, 2028 is a long way away, but it's not that far away. And I think this writ large makes Newsom, who is already struggling with somewhat of a likability problem, potentially more unlikable. I mean, this was his campaign manager's wife, who he was supposedly close with. And so even though he was divorced, again, of course, she was a subordinate. So, it's just -- it's not a -- it's not a great look. But how that plays moving forward, I mean, remains to be seen.

HILL: We -- I heard you start to say something over here.

SEAWRIGHT: Well, I was just going to say, all of these potential presidential candidates are going to get their hood checked and their tires kicked extensively by the American people between now and the 2028 primaries, where South Carolina will kick off on the political season for us.

But I will say, if you think about it, on the whole, remember, Donald Trump is the president of the United States. So, some of this stuff that was once mainstream priority and would have been an automatic disqualifier, I don't think the environment is reflective of that in this moment. And I think that's important to note. Otherwise, Trump would never be president.

HILL: Is it -- oh, go ahead, Rob.

BLUEY: Well, the -- I was going to say, the only problem with that is that Democrats, as you saw both during the Me Too movement and then, as Antjuan said, you know, in contrast with President Trump, they tried to make this one of the issues, that they are different. And so, I think not only in a Democratic primary you could have a contrast that some candidates try to make with Gavin Newsom.

But I also think that ultimately, and I think Eleanor's right on this, people are going to examine his record as governor of California, which has been disastrous. I mean, people are fleeing that state because of the high taxes, because of the homelessness problem, the drug problem. And you can go down the list, the wildfires. I mean, it has been a disaster from the point that he took office up until today. And that's probably going to be ultimately what does him in, I would think. And the more he talks, quite frankly, it seems that he keeps dropping precipitously in the polls.

HILL: We have like a minute left, so we barely have time for the group chat. Can you all share the time?

Eleanor, you're first.

MUELLER: My group chat was actually Rob's original group chat.

HILL: I know, you guys, but you can share.

MUELLER: Which was the amazing news we got yesterday that maybe the Dulles people movers are no more. If you don't live in D.C., they are these building like busses that take you from your gate to the baggage claim. They take forever. They are bulky and annoying and infamously hated and potentially --

HILL: I -- yes, I haven't experienced them. But I have to say, in looking at them, I'm happy for you all.

MUELLER: Thank you so much.

HILL: I mean, as someone who's based in New York, obviously, I don't use that airport much. When I come here I use DCA. But I am happy for you.

BLUEY: Get rid of them. Yes. Well, I -- so I pivoted and Aaron Rodgers, the 42-year-old quarterback for the Pittsburgh Steelers announced in training camp yesterday that this would be his final season.

I'm headed to Latrobe, Pennsylvania, next week to see the Steelers. So, I can't wait.

SEAWRIGHT: Max Miller, the son-in-law of Bernie Moreno, senator from Ohio, is on record in court filings for putting a gun to his wife's head, fracturing her collarbone, scalding her with hot water. But yet the party of family values and the Republicans have said or done nothing about it. In my group chat.

HILL: We have to end on that group chat because we have five seconds left. But on a happier note, have a great day. Thank you, guys. Appreciate you bringing it, as always.

Thanks to all of you for joining us. I'm Erica Hill. The headlines are next.

Iran Launches "Surprise Attack", U.S.-Saudi Strike Iran Proxies; 28 Million People Across Northeast Under Flood Watches; CNN Poll: 73 Percent Say Trump Not Paying Attention To Most Important Issues. Aired 6-6:30a ET

Aired July 29, 2026 - 06:00   ET

THIS IS A RUSH TRANSCRIPT. THIS COPY MAY NOT BE IN ITS FINAL FORM AND MAY BE UPDATED.

BRAD SMITH, CNN ANCHOR: Now also in California, a man was arrested after stealing a backhoe and then taking it on a Sunday morning joyride. It was all caught on camera here, as the witness says that the driver knocked down street signs and trees, all while the shirtless man was arrested. Okay, so some street signs and trees, all while the shirtless man was arrested.

Okay, so some interesting -- I can't even say maneuvering here ultimately, but some cleanup work for sure to be done there.

That does it for "CNN HEADLINE EXPRESS". I'm Brad Smith.

CNN THIS MORNING WITH AUDIE CORNISH starts right now

ERICA HILL, CNN ANCHOR: This just in. Nearly three out of four Americans polled by CNN say the president is not paying attention to the country's most important problems. And does that offer the GOP an impossible spot heading into the midterms?

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I don't think it's clicking that were being outpaced by our basic necessities -- groceries, gas, mortgage, living expenses.

HILL: The breaking news this morning, a surprise attack and questions about the timing. Could the U.S. and Iran be about to fall back into full scale war?

Life-threatening flash floods, storms packing a major punch in the Northeast. We're tracking that dangerous weather as it rolls through and the aftermath.

Dr. Anthony Fauci about to be grilled on Capitol Hill. His secret diary exposed for the world to read. So just what will we learn in this latest face off between Fauci and Rand Paul? Plus, workers at the biggest, world's biggest A.I. companies now

sounding the alarm about their technology. Why they say the development needs to slow down. But will anyone listen?

SAM ALTMAN, CEO, OPENAI: We are about to create a genie that can grant any wish.

HILL: President Trump wanted to give diplomacy another shot, but after a surprise attack from Iran, could the U.S. be doomed to repeat this bitter war cycle?

Good morning, everyone. I'm Erica Hill, in for Audie Cornish.

We do begin with the breaking news this hour, that new bombardment after days of relative calm in the Middle East. The U.S. and Saudi Arabia teaming up to hit back, targeting Iranian backed militias in Iraq. All of this after Iran tried to launch what the U.S. is calling a surprise missile attack on U.S. bases.

Now, all of those missiles were intercepted when military analysts says the timing here is key. Coming with Benjamin Netanyahu, of course, in Washington, D.C.

CEDRIC LEIGHTON, CNN MILITARY ANALYST: The Iranians see Israel and the U.S. get back together, and the Iranians see this as being a major issue in terms of continuing the war. They see that as basically the potential for a hostile act against them.

HILL: The attack, of course, coming at this crucial moment, President Trump trying to decide between negotiations or potentially further military action.

DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: For some reason, for some reason, we can be in the midst of a beautiful discussion and they'll come out and say, we're not talking or we didn't discuss nuclear.

ESMAIL BAGHAEI, IRANIAN FOREIGN MINISTRY SPOKESPERSON: No, do not pay much attention to the media speculation. As I said, we currently have no negotiations with America.

HILL: CNN business correspondent Eleni Giokos, who of course, has been covering this conflict from the very beginning, joining us now from Dubai. So, Eleni, when we look at this attack, the surprise attack as its

being labeled, those missiles intercepted. Saudi Arabia, though now joining in taking part in these joint attacks with the United States. Is there a sense there in the region that this is, in fact, trending toward a broader scale of the war?

ELENI GIOKOS, CNN BUSINESS CORRESPONDENT: That is exactly what the fear is, because we've got one -- on one hand, President Trump saying they're talking. Iran says they are not. And then Iran surprise attack against Jordan in the early hours of this morning.

And this is really significant because U.S. CENTCOM says they were able to intercept all those drones and missiles. But that just gives you a sense of where Iran is at. It wants to show that it has the missile and military capability to continue targeting Gulf states.

And then, importantly, you mentioned Saudi Arabia. Now, the Iranian proxy groups have been activated and mobilized. The Houthis, which are in Yemen targeting Saudi Arabia. Over the weekend, Saudi Arabia responding on Houthi held territory in Yemen.

And then just the beginning of this week, we saw Iranian backed Iraqi militia targeting key oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, as well as targeting the capital city Riyadh. Saudi Arabia decides to join forces with CENTCOM targeting eastern parts of Iraq. And they say it was precision targets. We know that the militants that are in Iraq, they say it resulted in 20 deaths, as well as 32 injuries.

But it certainly gives you a sense of how this is already broadening, bringing in other actors in terms of new threats that have emerged, Erica.

HILL: You talk about those other actors. There are also questions about the timing. As I noted, of course, President Trump meeting with Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the White House yesterday. They were calling it a positive meeting. There has certainly been a shift, though, in terms of what we see with the readouts after those meetings.

Israel's defense minister, Israel Katz, also talking about where things stand, but saying there's still some differences, quote, "We very much want to strike Iran's energy targets." The U.S. is not approving it at this time, based on the early reaction from this surprise attack, is there also a concern in the region that the U.S. perhaps may be leaning more toward that? President Trump, of course, talking about how he could, in his words, take out bridges, you know, take out infrastructure across Iran.

GIOKOS: Yeah. And that's such a good question, because President Trump's language over the past week and in fact, when the United States was targeting infrastructure and key sites in Iran for 13 consecutive nights, had warned that they could take out bridges and they would target power plants if the Strait of Hormuz doesn't fully reopen, and if the IRGC continues targeting vessels. Interesting to note that the Israeli defense minister says that Israel

still wants to target key energy infrastructure, but the United States is not on board with that. And we also know that President Trump, over the weekend huddled with advisors, and they were worried about the consequences. And then there was also concern about depleting munitions. So all of that playing a key role. And gulf states are very concerned because Iran has also said that they will escalate and target key gulf states should the United States make good on the threat to target bridges.

So, very tentative right now. The timing, as you say, super important here. And Iran seems to be wanting to set the tone and the pace in terms of what happens, whether it comes to peace and war, it is explicitly said so.

And then I'm looking at oil prices, Erica, and we've seen some massive moves. I mean, it hit $100 a barrel on Brent Crude on Friday, dropped dramatically. And then this morning again up 4 percent. It just shows the uncertainty that has been injected into this region and into the global market.

HILL: Yeah, absolutely. Eleni, really good to have you with us this morning. Appreciate it. Thank you.

We are keeping a close watch as well on this severe weather in the U.S., more than 20 million Americans facing the potential for life- threatening flash floods. We're talking about New England, including the city of Boston. Of course, New York as well.

A little bit further to the south, those areas expected to be hit hard again, the storm is creeping northeast after soaking parts of Pennsylvania on Tuesday. In Cumberland County, you can see here the water just turning streets into rivers in many areas.

Some spots of New Jersey, six inches of rain documented. This is from the city of Orange, New Jersey. More than a dozen cars and trucks underwater there.

CNN meteorologist Allison Chinchar joining me with the threat today.

I keep getting the alerts on my phone that I always get from New York City about emergency management, when there is weather incoming.

There are a lot of them at this point. How much more are we looking at in terms of the severe weather?

ALLISON CHINCHAR, CNN METEOROLOGIST: I think that's the key that it's not over just yet. You see videos like this, this one out of Pennsylvania, all of that water just kind of flowing through people's yards as well as streets and things like that. But now we're going to be adding more water on top of it.

So, when you look at the radar, you notice that this is not done yet. We still have some areas dealing with rain and in some cases very heavy rain even this morning. Here's a wider scope of this system as a whole. You can kind of see it as it slides to the north and east along this region.

Again, still some heavy rain just in the eastern boroughs of New York. We've also got very heavy rain across portions of Connecticut, and it's starting to slide into areas of Massachusetts and Rhode Island, in areas of Vermont.

You've got a lot of these red boxes here. Those are all the flash flood warnings that we have, indicating that we've not only had a lot of rain already fall, but more rain is continuing to fall in these areas.

Look at some of this. This is just since Monday. Focus here on a lot of these red shaded areas. That's where you're looking at least five to six inches of rain that has already come down. And you saw from that radar, we have even more that's going to continue, not just in the next hour or two, but really through the remainder of the day today.

Here's a look at what we've got. Again, almost five inches, almost six inches, six inches down through here. Again, you've got a lot of these areas that the ground is already saturated. So, at this point, its really not going to take all that much going for the remainder of the day today, before we start to see some additional flooding.

So, all of this area that you see here in green, this is where we have the flood watches, meaning the potential is there for additional flooding. The red boxes, again, those flash flood warnings, meaning flooding is already ongoing. You need to seek higher ground. Those kind of scenarios for that particular location.

This is the excessive rainfall risk for today. So, the highest target zone or where we really anticipate seeing the highest threat for flooding is going to be in this red shaded area here. However, anywhere in the yellow shaded area or even the green, if you get lined up in some of those thunderstorms, the really strong bands that just keep training over the same place over and over again, you could also see the potential for flooding.

So that's why really, anywhere you see highlighted on this map has that potential. There is a lot of moisture that is being pulled up into this region.

So that's why that concern is still there for the remainder of the day, just in anticipation of what we can expect.

HILL: All right. Allison, appreciate it. Thank you.

Ahead here on CNN THIS MORNING, the desperate search for survivors. Japanese rescue crews looking for people trapped inside a mall following that massive earthquake.

Plus, a longtime feud coming to a head in just a matter of hours. Dr. Fauci returning to the Hill where he will face Senator Rand Paul. And he's got 99 problems. And according to new polling, President

Trump may be ignoring the most important ones. The group chat has thoughts, next.

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: The fact that I'm at the dollar store grocery shopping because I can't afford to go to a regular grocery store is a problem in itself.

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I'm filling up my tank every three to four business days. Three to four business days!

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Our paychecks do not cover what we need to survive.

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: This economy is crap.

HILL: It is no secret millions of Americans are struggling right now to pay their bills, to put food on the table. Increasingly, they are blaming President Trump.

We have new polling just in here at CNN that reveals 73 percent of Americans now believe the president has not paid enough attention to the country's most important problems. Even Trump friendly Fox News sees trouble ahead for Republicans in the midterms.

BRIT HUME, FOX NEWS POLITICAL ANALYST: Underwater on the economy, as you showed. Underwater on affordability. Those two issues are front and center for sure, with the unpopular incumbent in this particular presidency in its first midterm. The weight of history is pretty strong. And the party in power in the White House has historically, with very few exceptions, done very poorly in the midterm like this one.

HILL: Joining me this morning in the group chat, Eleanor Mueller, White House economic policy reporter at "Semafor"; Rob Bluey, president and executive editor at "The Daily Signal". And Antjuan Seawright, Democratic strategist.

Nice to see all of you this morning.

When we look at this polling, there really are very few bright spots for the president or Republicans, frankly, heading into November. Where does the GOP focus, Eleanor, we're looking at numbers like these. ELEANOR MUELLER, WHITE HOUSE ECONOMY POLICY REPORTER, SEMAFOR: It's a

great question. And from talking to Republicans on Capitol Hill, they've told us they want to focus on their tax legislation, which was passed last year. It had tax breaks on overtime for seniors.

But of course, I mean, that conversation has gotten harder and harder to carry forward into the election cycle. And most notably, we saw that tension when the House and Senate passed a housing affordability bill and Trump publicly came out and said, I don't like this. I'm not going to sign it. And Republican leaders had to fight hard to get him not to veto it.

And so, there is this ongoing, intensifying, again, tension between Republicans whose incumbents are facing difficult elections across the country because of this sentiment. And then the president, who is increasingly focused really on his legacy and what he's going to leave behind.

HILL: You mentioned bipartisan housing bill. I believe the president called it a big yawn. Could have been a big win for Republicans in terms of what they could tout in terms of accomplishments heading into November. That can't happen in the same way. When we look at the approval rating to this is Trump's lowest number since just after the January 6th insurrection.

There was also polling from CBS News over the weekend, 78 percent think the administration there isn't focused enough on lowering prices. I mean, we are seeing this consistency across the polling.

Here's what the president had to say on Monday.

TRUMP: But we had the greatest economy in the history of the country, and we're blowing it away this time. We're blowing it away. You're going to see the results very soon.

HILL: Rob, Americans are very clear. We are not blowing it away. The president doesn't hear that. We know how that's gone for presidents past. See 2024.

How much longer can he stay on this road?

ROB BLUEY, PRESIDENT AND EXECUTIVE EDITOR, THE DAILY NEWS: Yeah. I think it's really important, Erica, to do a few things. Number one, wrap up the war in Iran. I think the American people want the president focused on the domestic issues that Eleanor was talking about.

And I think that the other thing that the members of Congress can do, in addition to selling the one big, beautiful bill, the working families tax cuts, as they now call it, is to pass this reconciliation bill. The White House signaled yesterday they want to expand the scope of that beyond what the House did. I think that's an encouraging sign. So, you can include things like the cost of housing, the cost of health care, the bread and butter issues that Americans are feeling pain right now when they go to the grocery store or fill up their gas tank.

Those are the types of issues they want President Trump talking about. They probably want to hear Republicans at town hall meetings over the course of August talking about. And I think that the more they can return to those issues, the better off they'll be come November.

ANTJUAN SEAWRIGHT, DEMOCRATIC STRATEGIST: Well, it's clear to me is that Donald Trump and the Republicans are not interested in having a relationship with the truth when it comes. That's called a lie, where I'm from.

When it comes to how Americans feel about the economic conditions, forget about the fact that Americans are trying to put ends together, hoping they meet because of Donald Trump's MAGA-nomics being a failure.

The reality is you have 25 million Americans paying more for their premiums, co-pays, and deductibles. That includes 18.2 million Americans in red states. You have the largest transfer of wealth in American history in the big ugly bill that Rob mentioned, including the largest cut to SNAP and Medicaid in American history.

Republicans can run, but they cannot hide. Americans are going to demonstrate their frustrations, their economic anxiety, and the economic uncertainty that Republicans have caused in November.

And you're starting to see a preview of that in the polling.

Every single major issue the president ran on in the last election cycle. And Republicans, they are underwater with the American people. And I think you see that poll after poll.

HILL: It is interesting where were seeing the president losing ground to specifically on immigration. That was really -- I mean, we're seeing that in this poll as well. That was a winning issue. He's also losing support from interesting voices, I will put it that way.

Alex Jones among them. Take a listen to this.

ALEX JONES, HOST, THE ALEX JONES SHOW: The big issue is how to stop Trump. And we have to have Congress go for the war powers. They three times tried to vote war powers. They're supposed to authorize a war.

This is a war. They're getting the draft ready. If this isn't a war, nothing's a war. I mean, this is absolutely out of control.

And so I'm calling for it right now, 25th Amendment, impeachment, whatever needs to happen to get this front and center.

HILL: Twenty-fifth Amendment. I mean, he talks about, Rob, you mentioned the war. The president needs to wrap up the war 28 percent, just 28 percent approve of the president's handling of the situation in Iran.

Do you think any of this, though, will actually change? To Rob's point, what he needs to talk about? Will it actually change any of that?

MUELLER: That is the question, right? And I think that is inherent to this new brand of populism that Trump has really brought to the Republican Party, is this conflict between saying, you're going to focus on America first, focus on improving peoples lives here in the U.S., but then also doing some of these traditionally Republican things, like focusing, for example, on tax cuts instead of spending on stuff like care policies.

And so, you know, as far as what that change is moving forward, I don't know that it changes anything in the Middle East. I do think it will increase the likelihood that he continues, for example, to lash out at the Federal Reserve, you know, pointing the finger at the Central Bank that he wants to blame for high mortgage rates instead of looking at what he's doing with the Iran war that's boosting prices. And so we'll see other ways that spells out.

SEAWRIGHT: The good news is November is coming, and Democrats have made a central core tenet or theme for this fall is were fighting for an affordable America that includes getting rid of the corruption and the crooks, holding them accountable. That means restoring the cuts, and that means saving health care.

Three central tenets, three central components that the American people, I believe, are tuned into and will vote for Democrats for in the fall.

BLUEY: All the more reason for Republicans to do something now while they have control of the House and Senate, Erica. Because if they lose that ability to legislate in the future, they're not going to get back this window where they have control in Washington.

SEAWRIGHT: They've had -- they've had two -- they've had two years to do it. Republicans control all branches of the government, and they have failed the American people in every which way they can.

HILL: We are going to leave that chat here, but there is much more chatting to come, as you -- as you all know.

Ahead after the break, is it actually time to rein in A.I.? The stark warning from A.I. developers and why they say it's not their job to fix it?

Plus, Todd Blanche's A.G. nomination uncertain. Could a key Republican be the one holding things up?

And how about a live look for you here. These are rivers of lava flowing from Kilauea Volcano, some shooting into the sky as you see there. It is erupting right now in Hawaii.

ALTMAN: We may have to pace the rate of ai development to give ourselves enough time for society to harden around some of these new capability levels.

HILL: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman admitting it may be time to hit the brakes as A.I. development accelerates faster than many experts are prepared for, the call for pacing the frontier coming just days after the world learned two OpenAI models went rogue and hacked outside companies, essentially breaking out of a testing lab earlier this month.

Now, more than 1,000 employees from leading artificial intelligence companies are weighing in, signing a letter that includes this warning, quote, there's a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.

Joining me now, Maria Curi, "Axios" tech policy reporter.

Really comforting when you see that in the letter, I have to be honest. I mean, this is sort of the -- what we saw with that model going rogue, right? That was the A.I. nightmare that a lot of non-A.I. people had, right?

MARIA CURI, TECH POLICY REPORTER, AXIOS: Right.

HILL: That this technology is just going to get too strong for everybody. And now we're in this moment. I mean, how concerned should we actually be?

CURI: You know, it's really interesting because Sam Altman, I remember in 2023 when he was on Capitol Hill asking lawmakers to impose a licensing regime on A.I. He has been saying for years now that this technology should be slowed down. And yet his company, as well as his competitors, continue to release these models at a very fast pace because they're feeling the heat and the competition from China.

And so, we're seeing now the technology is getting more and more powerful. We're seeing incidents like these where rogue agents are hacking into other companies. And at the end of the day, that's not -- that concern is not superseding the competition that these companies are feeling from China.

HILL: It's not. And so, as we see all of this play out, right? And for the China element of it, the fact that Hugging Face was the company, right? CURI: That's right.

HILL: That they actually used an open source model from China, correct, to get around or to -- or to rein in the other model going rogue, raised another question about the battle between the U.S. and China.

CURI: That's really key, because right now, one of the biggest debates that's unfolding in Washington is should we restrict open source versus closed source models?

We've seen the most alarming use cases happen from the closed source models. And so, when you have a lot of these companies lobbying the administration, not necessarily to get rid of open source, but to be more strict on it, it begs the question, what is the strategy there if safety is the end goal?

HILL: Well, also in terms of the strategy of safety as the end goal -- I mean, there's a certain amount of -- you read this letter, right?

MARIA CURI, AXIOS TECH POLICY REPORTER: Seen that the most alarming use cases have been from the closed source models. ERICA HILL, CNN ANCHOR: Well, also in terms of the strategy if safety is the end goal, I mean there's a certain amount of, you read this letter, right? And just -- a few other parts in this letter. So, it's signed by lead scientists at Google, Meta, Anthropic, OpenAI, a number of companies. Among the greatest hits, if you will, A.I. could help create a dramatically better future, but that outcome isn't guaranteed. We start off that way and go on to say, "we need to build a way for us all to slow down." Safety teams at A.I. companies have to sprint to prevent new risks to society every few months. Developing a technology shouldn't require a leap of faith for our continued survival." And perhaps my favorite, "if a rogue superintelligence is created, the game won't be chess."

I mean it feels like the people who created this are all admitting now they can't control it. So, they want government -- and, by the way, you're going to rely on government that doesn't even understand the technology -- to put in place the guardrails. It just feels -- it feels a little icky.

CURI: That doesn't understand the technology and that is not investing financially or with the technical expertise in the agencies that would understand the technology. And in terms of this rhetoric that we've been hearing for years now from these top A.I. CEOs. You know, the other side of that, the flip side of that is, a lot of skepticism. If they're speaking this way about the technology in order to do a sort of regulatory capture where they continue to benefit from dominating the market --

CURI: And they close out smaller players that can't adhere to these government rules and regulations.

HILL: That's part of it, too. But then you also, you know, from the outsider perspective, you have these companies saying, hey, we've created this technology. We're not actually capable of reining it in. And they're still going to keep developing it. But we're saying you should be the ones to fix it. It feels a little disingenuous.

CURI: On top of that, the promise of A.I., the, why are we doing all of this in the first place when it's being communicated to the average American is very pie in the sky right now. You know, it's going to cure cancer. It's going to solve climate change. But all Americans are feeling in the short term is actually an impact on their wallets, whether it's electricity, whether it's chips being more expensive, which means our phones and our computers are more expensive.

CURI: I just saw, you know, CNN recently reported nearly $400 increase per household directly related to all of the trillions of dollars that are being poured into artificial intelligence.

HILL: Right. And there are concerns about the data centers, the resources that they're taking up, right? The short-term benefit of perhaps some jobs to the long-term concerns, jobs being taken. There's a lot in here.

The good news, this is keeping you employed --

HILL: Because you're going to have plenty to talk about and explain to the rest of us. Really good to see you this morning. Thank you.

CURI: You as well. Thanks.

HILL: Straight ahead this morning, it is a scene out of "Mean Girls." Sort of burn book-esque, but in this case it's the diary dropped just before Dr. Anthony Fauci returns to The Hill. So, what are the actual revelations amidst the pettiness?

Plus, a close call at takeoff. Two Delta jets directed to turn around -- to turn in front of each other.

And fires burning with the intensity of, get this, several atomic bombs. How the extreme heat is further complicating efforts to contain those massive blazes in France and Spain.

HILL: Good morning, everyone. Thirty-seven minutes past the hour here on CNN THIS MORNING. Here's a look at what's happening right now.

Rescue workers searching through the rubble of a mall in Japan after that 6.8 magnitude quake hit yesterday. At least three people were found dead in that structure. A number of others, though, remain unaccounted for. The mall itself partially collapsed after an explosion, which was sparked by the quake. At least 13 people are confirmed dead in the region in connection with the earthquake.

A close call between two Delta planes in Atlanta after they were directed to turn in front of each other.

ATC: 1568 clear to land.

DL 1568: Somebody on the runway?

ATC: He's exiting now.

DEL 1568: Delta 1568, going around.

HILL: So, one plane was attempting to land while the other was taking off. The second plane decided to circle the runway. That, though, put the jet directly in front of the plane leaving the runway. Anti- collision alarms did blare in both planes. The air traffic controller then safely directed the two aircrafts away from one another.

Acting Attorney General Tom Blanche heading to Capitol Hill today where he's expected to meet with Senator John Cornyn after the Texas Republican said he may not support Blanche's nomination.

REPORTER: Would you recommend that it be postponed if it's going this way?

SEN. JOHN CORNYN (R-TX): That's being discussed. That's being discussed. But hopefully it won't be necessary.

HILL: Cornyn's issue, the DOJ's anti-weaponization fund. He is demanding the Justice Department provide a written proposal on how it plans to kill it once and for all.

Also happening on The Hill today, just about two hours from now, Dr. Anthony Fauci will head to Capitol Hill, where he's set to face a grilling by the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. That committee is led by Senator Rand Paul, who has butted heads with Fauci in past hearings over his role leading the nation's response to the Covid-19 pandemic. In the days leading up to this hearing, later this morning, the committee published 1,100 pages from Fauci's personal diary, detailing everything from high level White House pandemic meetings, to his newfound fame and press attention.

Fauci is not appearing voluntarily after Senator Paul previously called for the doctor to be thrown in jail.

SEN. RAND PAUL (R-KY): I would just suggest that he tell the truth. And if he tells the truth, he has no liability. But I would suggest that he testify because -- because he is protected by the pardon, there's no real constitutional reason for him not to testify.

HILL: The group chat is back with us.

I will note, there is a lot in here. As I noted, there are more than 1,100 pages. It's a little choose your own adventure, if you will, depending on what you are looking for in the diaries of Dr. Fauci.

Here is one thing that he wrote about a meeting in March of 2020, writing, quote, "we met with POTUS in the living quarters, not the Oval, for about an hour. I led the discussion since the POTUS kept referring to me. It was a disturbingly rambling discussion. He kept talking about TV ratings and HC and influenza and virtually everything else as I was trying to keep him on track with the help of the VP. We finally got him to agree to a travel advisory, not a quarantine."

As I noted, there is a little bit of something in here for everybody. We know it's going to be contentious with Rand Paul. But how are Democrats, do you think, going to approach this hearing today, Antjuan?

ANTJUAN SEAWRIGHT, DEMOCRATIC STRATEGIST: First of all, you had Trump's former surgeon general, I think as late as this morning, come out and praise Dr. Fauci and called him basically a trusted and good public servant.

But I think what's frustrating and what burns my biscuits the most is you have this political theater that will happen in the United States Senate today with Senator Rand Paul, but there's no interest in the fact that you have the screw worm sending everyone on the run. The fact that you see recall after recall in foods that basic, everyday Americans are afraid to even deal with, and all of the challenges that came along -- that come along with this current administration. And there's no sense of accountability in that regard.

I think that is what the American people are focused on, not in retrospect, but they're focused on right now in front of them. And right now in front of them are the challenges because of the people who are in charge of our government, but yet there's no accountability from a legislative standpoint. And so the theater is just going to be political theater for today. And I think the American people are -- have grown numb to some of that.

HILL: And then you think people move on. Rob does not feel that way.

ROB BLUEY, PRESIDENT AND EXECUTIVE EDITOR, "THE DAILY SIGNAL": Yes. No, I -- you can probably tell that I don't. I mean, I think that there will be fireworks today. I agree with you on that point. But it's the role of Congress, in this case Senator Rand Paul, to have oversight and hold this government employee, former government employee who was paid $400,000 a year with our tax dollars and who lied to the American people repeatedly about the origin of Covid. I mean he talked about --

SEAWRIGHT: How -- but, Rob -- but, Rob -- but, Rob, respectfully, how do you know that? And I -- we -- we --

BLUEY: Because it's in the diary.

SEAWRIGHT: Well, here's what we agree on. We agree that the legislative branch is supposed to have oversight and accountability to the executive branch. We agree with that. So, where's the accountability for the screw worm? Where's the accountability for all these recalls we see every single day and the lack thereof from the current leaders of our government. And you do not see that, but you want to focus on someone who's no longer in the government?

BLUEY: Oh, I'm a big champion of the Article One authority of Congress. So, don't -- we can go down that path. I think Congress should exert more authority when it comes to oversight, whether it's a Republican or a Democrat.

But I think what is important today, and the reason that it's relevant, is, this might not be the last time that the United States finds itself in a situation where we have a global pandemic. And holding that person accountable, getting answers, holding the CCP, the Chinese Communist Party, accountable for what its role was. And then think about all of the losses that our country experienced, not only in terms of jobs, but the schooling. I mean, I have kids. It affected my family's life profoundly.

SEAWRIGHT: Can someone remind me who was in charge when we were going through the Covid-19 pandemic? Because I think sometimes that gets lost in the conversation. Who was the president?

BLUEY: Apparently, Anthony Fauci thought he was.

SEAWRIGHT: Well, who was in charge and who was the president?

HILL: I want to bring -- so I want to -- because I know you two could go on all day, and I do enjoy it. Don't get me wrong.

But, Eleanor, when we look at this, right, people, to Rob's point, people do have questions, right? To Antjuan's point, people are also questioning certain things that are happening right now.

When we look at what has come out in advance, there is no love lost between Rand Paul and Anthony Fauci, as we know.

ELEANOR MUELLER, WHITE HOUSE ECONOMY POLICY REPORTER, "SEMAFOR": Yes.

HILL: What does this -- what does this actually achieve, right, to put all this out ahead of time? And it is really, you can pick and choose who you want. It's certainly not all flattering to Dr. Fauci --

HILL: But it doesn't all either prove what Rand Paul, I think, is hoping to prove.

So, what do we, as the American people, get from this moment? MUELLER: So, for Americans, particularly on the right, who were

frustrated with lockdowns, who thought that guidance on vaccines was misplaced, Anthony Fauci was the place that they directed all of those frustrations into. And so, while there is nothing, to your point, in these 1,100 pages that RFK found on government servers and gave to Rand Paul that would incriminate Fauci, it does stoke those political tensions right as this fifth hearing that Rand Paul has called where he can interrogate Fauci is going to happen.

And so whether or not Fauci does do what Paul wants and says something today that does incriminate himself remains to be seen. I don't know that there's proof in these diaries that he does think that it came from a lab.

MUELLER: He made one comment that maybe alluded to the possibility of the lab being somehow related, but didn't explicitly say something that contradicted himself in the past. And so, it's really more of a bad look, I think, to have him leaning into all of this fame.

SEAWRIGHT: And remember --

HILL: Here's -- I'm going to leave it there because we have more to get to.

SEAWRIGHT: Trump was in charge of Covid.

HILL: But we have more to get to. But it will certainly -- I mean there will be, I think we can all guarantee, no shortage of fireworks this morning or moments that people would like to have go viral. So, we'll be watching all of it for you.

Still ahead here on CNN THIS MORNING, Gavin Newsom's affair with a then staffer reemerging two decades later. How the scandal could impact a potential presidential run.

SEN. RICHARD BLUMENTHAL (D-CT): America stands with Ukraine.

HILL: A win for Ukraine. The U.S. Senate passing a Russian sanctions bill. Can Ukraine's leader now turn this momentum into Patriot missiles?

And the lifeguard who dove into a pounding surf to rescue a boy set to receive a high civilian honor as President Trump offers an invite to the White House.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK) [06:50:41]

HILL: Breaking news overnight, an escalation in the war with Iran. The U.S. and Saudi Arabia joining forces to target Iranian backed militias in Iraq after Iran attempted to launch a surprise missile attack on U.S. bases in the region. Those missiles were intercepted. Iran making its move, of course, while Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, was in Washington, as well as Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, both visiting Trump at the White House on Tuesday.

Zelenskyy also in Washington making his way later in the day to The Hill to watch the U.S. advance -- the Senate advance a sanctions bill for Russia and Iran.

PRESIDENT VOLODYMYR ZELENSKYY, UKRAINE: It's not only about money, how Russia -- how to stop to finance this war, but it's also a big signal to Europe, a big signal to Ukraine, big support of our people.

HILL: Joining me now, David Sanger, White House and national security correspondent for "The New York Times."

DAVID SANGER, CNN POLITICAL AND NATIONAL SECURITY ANALYST: Good morning, Erica.

HILL: I mean, a lot happening in the last -- in the last 24 hours I think is putting it mildly when we look at what is happening on both fronts with Iran and Ukraine.

Let's start, though, if we could, with these attacks overnight and what we saw. The timing cannot be ignored, obviously, but also what has come out of that. The U.S. and Saudi Arabia joining forces now. Can you put this in perspective for us?

SANGER: Sure. So, you know, last time that we discussed this, Erica, we talked about how the president was increasingly trapped by his inability to get out of this war. And I think in the past 24 hours, we've seen why. He stood down over the weekend from what he had threatened would be a massive attack. It looked like we had some peace in the region for a bit. And then, four days into this, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which we believe is really running Iran these days, or is the most influential force there, launches this not very large attack, it was four or fewer missiles, that were at Jordan.

Meanwhile, the Saudis, tired of being attacked by the Houthis and some Iran-backed militias, did some airstrikes in Iraq. And so, you see that this is beginning to spread, or is continuing to spread throughout the region. And the more countries that get involved, the more difficult it gets to unwind this whole thing. So, the whole question right now for the president is, could he even

get the Iranians back to the position they were in a little more than a month ago when he signed that 14-point vaguely written plan that was supposed to launch a bigger negotiation.

HILL: All of this happening, of course, when Benjamin Netanyahu was visiting Washington. There is clearly a disconnect between the president and the prime minister when it comes to where this war goes, right, and what they each would like to see.

What is your takeaway from that meeting, what it says about this relationship right now, as the two are still involved in this war together?

SANGER: We don't know very much about what happened in the meeting yet. I'm sure more of that will begin to seep out. But we do know this. This was the first time the two of them had met since Prime Minister Netanyahu was in Washington prior to the war. And that was the time when he basically convinced President Trump that if they joined together in an attack on Iran, it would be swift, it would overthrow the government, that Iran was so weak that it would crack, and this would be a couple of weeks' operation.

Well, clearly, that turned out to be wrong. And I think the president is now rightly suspicious a bit of Prime Minister Netanyahu's predictions.

HILL: I also want to ask you about President Zelenskyy. So, of course, I noted he was there for, you know, in the Senate yesterday, but also meeting with the president, bringing some wins with him in this moment. You noted, he may actually have those cards now that the president gave him such a hard time about in that infamous Oval Office meeting. Does he have a lot more leverage in this moment?

SANGER: He sure does. And, you know, it really shows you what, you know, a year and a half of change, technological development and just grit will do here.

When he came in February of last year, he didn't have that many cards to play. He was, you know, at best static and maybe losing on the battlefield. They've now developed drones that obviously reach well into Russia, have done significant damage to the Russian oil and gas industry, hit a lot of their refineries, can reach Moscow. And suddenly it was President Zelenskyy who was getting a bit of a warmer reception than Prime Minister Netanyahu. How's that for a reversal of fortunes here?

Now, the president can be a little bit fickle on these things. And, of course, he likes sticking with winners. But it does raise the question of whether the U.S. and the Congress will end up doing more to back the Ukrainians as Lindsey Graham was advocating until his death.

HILL: Yes. It will certainly interesting to watch, as always.

David, always good to talk to you. Thank you.

SANGER: Great to be with you, Erica.

HILL: A former staffer to Gavin Newsom is offering new details of their affair from 20 years ago. Newsom, who at the time was the mayor of San Francisco, admitted to that affair in 2007. An affair with Ruby Rippey. But his rise as a potential 2028 presidential contender is putting this chapter in his life back in the spotlight. He also wrote about it in his book recently. And then in an essay published in "Vanity Fair" yesterday, Rippey says, "for my former boss, it is a footnote in a larger arc of ascent. For me, it is the fracture that split my life into before and after."

The group chat is back.

I will say, she writes in this this "Vanity Fair" piece, it's not written from a victim perspective, right, it's more of a, hey, I'm just letting you all know what happened in this moment. A spokesperson for Newsom put this message out in response, saying the governor had apologized for what had happened and noted that he was, you know, sort of done talking about it. He apologized for it. He's going to move on. He calls it in his memoir, "the briefest of affairs," and recounted how he claimed -- came clean to Rippey's husband, who also worked for Newsom at the time, and was a friend of the mayors. She points out, that's not actually what happened.

How much could this impact Newsom moving forward?

MUELLER: That's the question, right? I mean, 2028 is a long way away, but it's not that far away. And I think this writ large makes Newsom, who is already struggling with somewhat of a likability problem, potentially more unlikable. I mean, this was his campaign manager's wife, who he was supposedly close with. And so even though he was divorced, again, of course, she was a subordinate. So, it's just -- it's not a -- it's not a great look. But how that plays moving forward, I mean, remains to be seen.

HILL: We -- I heard you start to say something over here.

SEAWRIGHT: Well, I was just going to say, all of these potential presidential candidates are going to get their hood checked and their tires kicked extensively by the American people between now and the 2028 primaries, where South Carolina will kick off on the political season for us.

But I will say, if you think about it, on the whole, remember, Donald Trump is the president of the United States. So, some of this stuff that was once mainstream priority and would have been an automatic disqualifier, I don't think the environment is reflective of that in this moment. And I think that's important to note. Otherwise, Trump would never be president.

HILL: Is it -- oh, go ahead, Rob.

BLUEY: Well, the -- I was going to say, the only problem with that is that Democrats, as you saw both during the Me Too movement and then, as Antjuan said, you know, in contrast with President Trump, they tried to make this one of the issues, that they are different. And so, I think not only in a Democratic primary you could have a contrast that some candidates try to make with Gavin Newsom.

But I also think that ultimately, and I think Eleanor's right on this, people are going to examine his record as governor of California, which has been disastrous. I mean, people are fleeing that state because of the high taxes, because of the homelessness problem, the drug problem. And you can go down the list, the wildfires. I mean, it has been a disaster from the point that he took office up until today. And that's probably going to be ultimately what does him in, I would think. And the more he talks, quite frankly, it seems that he keeps dropping precipitously in the polls.

HILL: We have like a minute left, so we barely have time for the group chat. Can you all share the time?

Eleanor, you're first.

MUELLER: My group chat was actually Rob's original group chat.

HILL: I know, you guys, but you can share.

MUELLER: Which was the amazing news we got yesterday that maybe the Dulles people movers are no more. If you don't live in D.C., they are these building like busses that take you from your gate to the baggage claim. They take forever. They are bulky and annoying and infamously hated and potentially --

HILL: I -- yes, I haven't experienced them. But I have to say, in looking at them, I'm happy for you all.

MUELLER: Thank you so much.

HILL: I mean, as someone who's based in New York, obviously, I don't use that airport much. When I come here I use DCA. But I am happy for you.

BLUEY: Get rid of them. Yes. Well, I -- so I pivoted and Aaron Rodgers, the 42-year-old quarterback for the Pittsburgh Steelers announced in training camp yesterday that this would be his final season.

I'm headed to Latrobe, Pennsylvania, next week to see the Steelers. So, I can't wait.

SEAWRIGHT: Max Miller, the son-in-law of Bernie Moreno, senator from Ohio, is on record in court filings for putting a gun to his wife's head, fracturing her collarbone, scalding her with hot water. But yet the party of family values and the Republicans have said or done nothing about it. In my group chat.

HILL: We have to end on that group chat because we have five seconds left. But on a happier note, have a great day. Thank you, guys. Appreciate you bringing it, as always.

Thanks to all of you for joining us. I'm Erica Hill. The headlines are next.

sentences.en: The U.S. and Saudi Arabia teaming up to hit back, targeting Iranian backed militias in Iraq.

sentences.structure: 主谓宾结构，现在分词短语作伴随状语
sentences.analysis: 主句为'The U.S. and Saudi Arabia teaming up to hit back'，其中'teaming up'是现在分词短语作谓语，'to hit back'是不定式作目的状语。逗号后'targeting Iranian backed militias in Iraq'是现在分词短语作伴随状语，补充说明行动的具体目标。

sentences.en: Now, all of those missiles were intercepted when military analysts says the timing here is key.

sentences.structure: 主谓被动结构，后接时间状语从句
sentences.analysis: 主句为'all of those missiles were intercepted'，被动语态。'when military analysts says the timing here is key'是时间状语从句，其中'says'应为'say'（主谓一致错误），从句中'the timing here is key'是宾语从句。

sentences.en: And then, importantly, you mentioned Saudi Arabia. Now, the Iranian proxy groups have been activated and mobilized.

sentences.structure: 并列句，第一句为简单句，第二句为现在完成时的被动语态
sentences.analysis: 第一句'you mentioned Saudi Arabia'是简单主谓宾结构。第二句'the Iranian proxy groups have been activated and mobilized'是现在完成时的被动语态，表示动作已完成且对现在有影响。

sentences.en: And then just the beginning of this week, we saw Iranian backed Iraqi militia targeting key oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, as well as targeting the capital city Riyadh.
sentences.cn: 然后就在本周初，我们看到伊朗支持的伊拉克民兵瞄准了沙特阿拉伯的关键石油基础设施，以及首都利雅得。
sentences.structure: 主谓宾结构，后接现在分词短语作宾语补足语
sentences.analysis: 主句为'we saw Iranian backed Iraqi militia'，'targeting key oil infrastructure...'是现在分词短语作宾语补足语，描述民兵的行动。'as well as targeting the capital city Riyadh'是并列结构，补充另一个目标。

sentences.en: But it certainly gives you a sense of how this is already broadening, bringing in other actors in terms of new threats that have emerged, Erica.

sentences.structure: 主谓宾结构，后接宾语从句和现在分词短语
sentences.analysis: 主句为'it certainly gives you a sense'，'of how this is already broadening'是介词短语作定语修饰'sense'，其中'how this is already broadening'是宾语从句。'bringing in other actors...'是现在分词短语作结果状语，'that have emerged'是定语从句修饰'threats'。

sentences.cn: 他发表了一句评论，可能暗指实验室以某种方式相关，但没有明确说出与过去自相矛盾的话。
sentences.structure: 并列句，每个分句包含定语从句。
sentences.analysis: 第一个分句主语 He，谓语 made，宾语 one comment，that 引导定语从句修饰 comment。第二个分句 but 连接，省略主语，谓语 didn't say，宾语 something，that 引导定语从句修饰 something。

sentences.en: When he came in February of last year, he didn't have that many cards to play.
sentences.cn: 当他去年二月上任时，他没有那么多牌可打。
sentences.structure: 时间状语从句 + 主句。
sentences.analysis: When 引导时间状语从句，主句主语 he，谓语 didn't have，宾语 cards，不定式 to play 作定语。

sentences.en: They've now developed drones that obviously reach well into Russia, have done significant damage to the Russian oil and gas industry, hit a lot of their refineries, can reach Moscow.
sentences.cn: 他们现在开发了能够深入俄罗斯的无人机，对俄罗斯的石油和天然气工业造成了重大破坏，击中了许多炼油厂，并能到达莫斯科。
sentences.structure: 主句 + 定语从句，定语从句包含并列谓语。
sentences.analysis: 主句主语 They，谓语 have developed，宾语 drones，that 引导定语从句修饰 drones，从句中谓语并列：reach, have done, hit, can reach。

sentences.en: And suddenly it was President Zelenskyy who was getting a bit of a warmer reception than Prime Minister Netanyahu.
sentences.cn: 突然之间，泽连斯基总统受到的接待比内塔尼亚胡总理更热情一些。
sentences.structure: 强调句型。
sentences.analysis: It was... who... 是强调句型，强调主语 President Zelenskyy，who 引导定语从句修饰 Zelenskyy，从句中包含比较结构 warmer... than。

sentences.en: But it does raise the question of whether the U.S. and the Congress will end up doing more to back the Ukrainians as Lindsey Graham was advocating until his death.
sentences.cn: 但这确实提出了一个问题：美国国会是否会最终采取更多行动支持乌克兰人，正如林赛·格雷厄姆生前所倡导的那样。
sentences.structure: 主句 + 同位语从句 + 方式状语从句。
sentences.analysis: 主句主语 it，谓语 does raise，宾语 the question，of 后接 whether 引导的同位语从句。从句中包含 as 引导的方式状语从句。

sentences.en: And I think that ultimately, and I think Eleanor's right on this, people are going to examine his record as governor of California, which has been disastrous.
sentences.cn: 我认为最终，而且我认为埃莉诺在这点上是对的，人们会审视他作为加州州长的记录，这记录是灾难性的。
sentences.structure: 主句 + 宾语从句，宾语从句包含插入语和非限制性定语从句。
sentences.analysis: 主句 I think，后接 that 引导的宾语从句。从句中插入 and I think Eleanor's right on this，主谓 people are going to examine，宾语 his record，as governor of California 是同位语，which 引导非限制性定语从句修饰 record。

topics.title: 中东局势：伊朗与美国及盟友的冲突
